The Big-eye mandarin fish Siniperca knerii exhibits a life-history pattern shaped by its piscivorous feeding ecology and the seasonal thermal regime of its freshwater habitat. Egg diameter averages 1.2 mm, a value that yields a calculated wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0009 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0009 grams], placing the species within the range typical for predatory teleosts with pelagic eggs. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae rely entirely on endogenous reserves during the initial endotrophic phase, a period of rapid yolk absorption that precedes the critical transition to exogenous feeding. Upon completion of first exogenous feeding, the growing juveniles begin a phase of accelerated growth that continues through the sub-adult stage. Field growth studies indicate that the maximum total length attained by adults is 41.5 cm [Li = 41.5 cm], a size that corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 2282 grams [Wwi = 2282 grams] based on length-weight regressions derived from specimens collected across the species' range. This asymptotic body size is consistent with values reported for other large-bodied members of the Sinipercidae.

Pubertal development in Siniperca knerii is closely tied to the attainment of a specific body size rather than a strict chronological age. Analysis of gonadal recrudescence in a wild population from the Yangtze River basin revealed that the total length at puberty is 17 cm [Lp = 17 cm]. This length marks the onset of gametogenesis and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, though first reproduction typically occurs somewhat later. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, derived from the allometric relationship between length and mass, is 157 grams [Wwp = 157 grams]. This body mass threshold likely ensures that sufficient somatic reserves are available to support the energetic demands of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. Notably, individuals maturing at a smaller size than this threshold have been observed to produce fewer oocytes, suggesting a trade-off between early maturation and future fecundity.

Reproductive output in this species is comparatively high, a trait characteristic of many freshwater piscivores. At a stable water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], females produce an average of approximately 320,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 320,000 eggs per spawning event], based on a relative fecundity of 140 eggs per gram of body mass combined with an adult body mass of 2282 grams. Spawning occurs once per year [F_R_i = once per year], with gravid individuals releasing multiple batches of demersal adhesive eggs that become attached to submerged vegetation or rocky substrates. The high fecundity is offset by substantial egg mortality from fungal infection and predation, which is a common feature of demersal spawning strategies. Field observations indicate that spawning events are triggered by rising water temperatures in early spring, with peak activity occurring when thermal conditions remain near 21 °C.

Longevity in Siniperca knerii is moderate for a teleost of its ultimate body size, with otolith-based age estimates indicating that the maximum lifespan is 13 years [am = 13 years] when reared at 21 °C [T = 21 °C] under controlled conditions in a laboratory setting. This relatively prolonged lifespan, equivalent to approximately 4745 days, reflects a growth strategy characterized by sustained somatic investment even after the attainment of reproductive maturity. The oldest individuals are typically those occupying the most energetically profitable foraging territories, where access to abundant prey fish minimizes the metabolic costs associated with active hunting. In natural populations, senescence-related mortality becomes evident after approximately 10 years, with older females showing a marked decline in fecundity and egg viability. Comparative data suggest that the lifespan of this species is intermediate between short-lived zooplanktivorous cyprinids and long-lived predatory catfishes from the same river systems.

The relationship between size at puberty and ultimate size in this species follows the general allometric pattern described by the cube law for fish. Using the ratio of length at puberty to ultimate length, (17 cm / 41.5 cm) raised to the third power, the proportional mass at maturity is calculated to be approximately 6.9 percent of the ultimate wet weight. This value of 157 grams [Wwp = 157 grams] at 21 °C [T = 21 °C] places the Big-eye mandarin fish among species that delay reproduction until a relatively advanced stage of somatic development, a life-history strategy often associated with high juvenile survival and predictable adult food resources. The slow approach to asymptotic size means that most individuals spend several years as sub-adults before entering the spawning population. This ontogenetic delay carries the benefit of allowing females to accumulate sufficient lipid stores to produce multiple large egg batches over successive spawning seasons, thereby maximizing lifetime reproductive output.
